scenes.heading: Simulating chance with algorithms
scenes.sub: Roll a die a thousand times in one second
scenes.say: How do forecasters and game designers work out chances? They get a computer to act out the situation thousands of times with random numbers, and count what happens. That's a simulation. Let's build one.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A flight simulator lets pilots fly thousands of times on the ground
scenes.science: A simulation acts out a chance experiment thousands of times
scenes.breaks: A simulation only copies the probabilities. Set them up wrongly and every result is wrong, however many trials you run.
scenes.say: Think of a flight simulator. Pilots practise thousands of flights without leaving the ground. A chance simulation is the same idea for probability. But it only copies the probabilities, so if you set those up wrongly, every result is wrong.

scenes.heading: Match numbers to outcomes
scenes.say: First, match random numbers to outcomes. A fair die is RandInt one to six. For a probability of zero point three, use digits zero to nine, with zero, one and two meaning yes. For zero point three five, use zero zero to ninety-nine, with zero zero to thirty-four meaning yes. Always check: yes numbers divided by all numbers.
scenes.caption: Match random numbers to outcomes. A fair die is RandInt(1, 6). For 0.3, use digits 0–9 with 0, 1, 2 meaning yes. For 0.35, use 00–99 with 00–34 meaning yes. Check: yes numbers ÷ all numbers.

scenes.heading: Count, loop, test, output
scenes.say: Here's the algorithm as a flowchart. First the counter is set to zero. Then roll a die. If it's a six, add one to the count. Add one to the trials, and loop until a thousand trials are done. The output, count divided by trials, is the relative frequency.

scenes.heading: Free throws: 70% chance
scenes.question: Digits 0 to 6 = score, 7 to 9 = miss. Digits: 3 8 0 5 9 1 6 2 7 4
scenes.say: A basketballer scores seventy percent of free throws. Zero to six is seven digits out of ten, so the matching is right. Mark the scores: three, zero, five, one, six, two and four. That's seven out of ten, a relative frequency of zero point seven.
scenes.caption: A basketballer scores 70% of free throws. 0 to 6 is 7 digits out of 10, so the matching is right. Scores: 3, 0, 5, 1, 6, 2, 4. That's 7 out of 10: relative frequency 0.7.

scenes.heading: More trials, steadier estimate
scenes.say: This graph shows one run of a thousand rolls. First the axes, then the dashed line at one sixth. With only a few rolls, the relative frequency jumps all over the place. As the rolls pile up, it settles close to one sixth. That's why simulations use thousands of trials.
scenes.caption: One run of 1000 rolls. With only a few rolls, the relative frequency jumps around. As the rolls pile up, it settles close to 1/6. That's why simulations use thousands of trials.

scenes.heading: Expected count
parts: how many times you run it
scenes.say: To predict a count, multiply. Four hundred days with a rain chance of zero point three five gives about one hundred and forty rainy days. Real runs land near that, not exactly on it.
scenes.caption: To predict a count, multiply. 400 days × 0.35 = about 140 rainy days. Real runs land near that, not exactly on it.

points: Simulation = random numbers acting out chance
scenes.say: Quick recap. A simulation uses random numbers to act out chance. Match numbers so that yes numbers divided by all numbers equals the probability. Count, loop, test, output. More trials give a better estimate, and expected count is trials times probability. Now try the practice questions!
